cues.text: Let us turn now to coding quality, which is about how well code is written, not merely whether it runs.
We begin with two ideas that sound similar but are different.
Readability is about whether code is understandable.
Can another person, or you six months from now, open it and follow what it does?
Maintainability goes a step further.
It is about whether change is economical and safe.
In other words, when requirements shift, can you modify the code cheaply, without breaking things that already work?
So how do we achieve this?
The source gives us several practices.
First, use descriptive names, so that a variable, function or class tells you its purpose.
Second, use consistent formatting, so the code looks uniform across the project.
Third, write small, cohesive functions, each focused on one job.
Fourth, make contracts explicit, meaning that what a function expects and what it promises to return are clearly stated.
And fifth, write meaningful comments, specifically comments that explain why something is done, rather than repeating what the code already says.
Next come three short principles that are often quoted by their acronyms.
KISS avoids unnecessary complexity.
Keep the solution as simple as the problem allows.
DRY avoids duplicated knowledge.
Notice the precision here: it is about duplicated knowledge, not every similar line.
Two lines of code can look alike yet represent different ideas, and forcing them together is not what DRY asks for.
Then YAGNI avoids speculative features.
Do not build something just because you imagine you might need it someday.
Then we have SOLID, five design principles.
S is single responsibility.
O is open and closed.
L is Liskov substitution.
I is interface segregation.
And D is dependency inversion.
The source lists these by name, so make sure you can recall all five in order.
Two more ideas help here.
High cohesion and low coupling make modules easier to change and to test.
Cohesion describes how closely the parts inside one module belong together.
Coupling describes how strongly one module depends on others.
You want the first high and the second low.
Finally, refactoring.
Refactoring changes the internal structure of code without any intended change in observable behaviour.
From the outside, the software should act the same; only the inside is improved.
And tests support confidence, because they let you check that behaviour really did stay the same.
Now let us move to code review and related practices.
Code review serves several purposes.
It finds defects, finds security issues, surfaces design problems, and shares knowledge across the team.
To support review, use standards, linters and formatters.
Standards define the agreed conventions, while linters and formatters help check and apply them automatically.
Next, error handling, which should be done deliberately.
Validate input.
Distinguish expected business errors from unexpected failures.
An expected business error might be a rule being violated in normal operation, whereas an unexpected failure is something that should not normally happen.
Return an appropriate status.
Log structured context, together with correlation IDs, but without sensitive information.
A correlation ID lets you follow one request across the different parts of a system.
Clean up resources when you finish with them.
And avoid swallowing exceptions, which means do not catch an error and silently ignore it.
When something does go wrong, debugging follows a sequence.
First, reproduce the problem.
Second, inspect the logs and the stack trace.
Third, isolate the cause.
Fourth, fix it.
And fifth, add a regression test, so that the same defect cannot quietly return later.
Alongside this, logging, metrics and traces support observability.
That is, they help you understand what a running system is doing from the evidence it produces.
Our last block concerns Git and collaboration.
Git tracks snapshots and history of your work.
Commit small, meaningful changes.
Branch when team policy calls for parallel work.
Merge or rebase appropriately, resolve conflicts, and review.
Tag releases, so that a particular version can be identified later.
GitHub and GitLab host collaboration, reviews and pipelines.
And an important rule: never commit credentials or production datasets.
Finally, a distinction that is often confused.
A revert makes a new commit that undoes a change, which is useful for shared history because it does not rewrite what others have already seen.
A reset, by contrast, rewrites local state, and it can be destructive if misused.
